message.reasoning:
I need to decide whether to bid on Atlantic Avenue in the current auction.

I have $463 and a complete green group. Atlantic Avenue is worth $260 but only mortgages for $130. It does not complete the yellow group.

I will bid up to $130 for mortgage arbitrage and to secure two of the three yellows. I will drop out if the bid exceeds that amount.

I will bid $12 to stay in the auction. p3 has no yellows and will likely not raise the price. p4 can only afford a maximum bid of $74.

p4 would profit $56 from mortgaging the property after winning at $74. p3 could net $39 from a $91 bid. Denying them this arbitrage is a key strategic goal.

Blocking p1 from completing the yellow group is already partially achieved by holding Ventnor. Winning Atlantic would secure two of three yellows and prevent p1 from finishing the set.

The real danger is that p4 or p3 could win cheap and mortgage the property for a cash infusion. p4 has three houses on Boardwalk and Park Place, while p3 has four houses on the pink group. Denying them this free money is the most important strategic reason to stay in the auction.

I will use a minimum-raise strategy to push the bid up to each opponent's cash limit. This forces p4 to pay $74 and p3 to pay $91, while I secure the property for under $130.

If I win at $92, I would net $38 after mortgaging the property for $130. That leaves me with $371 in cash and a total of $501 once the mortgage is applied.

I will not mortgage the property immediately. The auction bid is separate from that decision.

Winning under $130 is strictly positive in expected value for liquidity, since mortgaging the property afterward yields $130 cash. The only risk is if p3 bids up to $91.

I will not jump to $75 to eliminate p4 immediately. A minimum raise is safer because p4 and p3 know the mortgage arbitrage from the earlier warning, so they may bid aggressively once they see my interest.
